newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Rental Cars Age.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Rental Cars Age.

text.p: Business travelers accustomed to taking the wheel of a factory-fresh rental car are finding something different -- cars that may be as much as a year old, some of them even purchased used by the rental companies.
On top of that, it may be increasingly hard to find a rental car in key markets at busy times in the coming year.
Donna Seehrman, vice president for hotel and car relations at American Express Corporate Services, says the change is rooted in the success Detroit has had selling American-made cars.

In earlier years when sales of U.S. models sagged, the manufacturers could dump the excess into the rental market, through marketing and ownership arrangements they have with the car rental companies.
The business provided a ready market for discount selling of inventory that might otherwise have stacked up.
"But with the increasing popularity of American-made cars, the companies have been pulling back on what they have been sending to the rental market, and raising costs," Seehrman said in an interview.
"That has resulted in less fleet availability and it has impacted the average age of the (rental) fleet," she added.

Both Ford and General Motors have cut back sales to rental companies. While six months used to be the average age for cars in a rental fleet, some cars are now being kept in service for a year, Seehrman said.
Some companies are supplementing their fleets with used cars, she added.
American Express in a recent business travel cost forecast for 1997, said the prices of rental cars to customers will rise by 4 percent to 5 percent, slightly more than they did in 1996.
"Where it was often easy to get a car as the last minute there are now markets where they will be sold out," Seehrman said. That is due in part to smaller growth in the size of fleets.
American Express estimates rental car fleets increased in size by about about 5 percent in 1996, a smaller growth rate than in past years.

On another front, travelers who have piled up frequent flier points know it is sometimes hard to turn them into free trips because of restrictions imposed by the airlines. There are only so many free seats available at any given time, and competition for the space has increased with the proliferation of programmes making it possible to earn mileage credit with everything from home loan refinancing to gift buying.
Consumer Reports Travel Letter provides some useful information on which carriers are the most likely to cash in points for a free trip.
Alaska, American, TWA and United were the most generous during 1995, the publication said, based on a formula that compares mileage credit available to trips actually offered
Continental and Delta were the stingiest, the newsletters said, while America West, Northwest and USAir were somewhere in between.
The letter's December issue provides a detailed rundown on that and the ins and outs of all frequent flier programmes. Information on the publication can be obtained at 1-800-234-1970.
